memory_update.text: AI should be treated as an infrastructure stack spanning compute, networking, optical, power, cooling, grid, and software automation rather than as a single semiconductor trade.
Optical interconnect manufacturing, photonics components, and precision substrates are high-priority underfollowed AI infrastructure nodes for later source-backed screening.
AI-server passive components and board-level power delivery, especially high-end MLCCs, deserve further research as a second-order component-intensity beneficiary.

Data-center power, thermal, switchgear, transformer, and grid-services suppliers are important AI bottleneck candidates, with smaller industrial suppliers likely more underfollowed than headline infrastructure names.

Layer 1B should build a public-company universe across optical EMS, photonics, passives, advanced packaging/test, power/thermal/grid, and AI workflow software, then verify revenue exposure and market attention.
Later layers must include falsification checks for customer concentration, insourcing, capex slowdown, qualification failure, capacity normalization, and valuation already pricing the bottleneck.

layer1a.summary: Layer 1A decomposes AI as a multi-lane infrastructure theme rather than a single GPU trade. The highest-quality next research lanes are: optical interconnect manufacturing and photonics capacity, high-density passive components and power delivery inside AI servers, advanced packaging and foundry capacity, data-center electrical and thermal infrastructure, AI software/workflow automation with measurable enterprise deployment, and nuclear/grid power availability. The underfollowed discovery angle should prioritize obscure suppliers one or two steps away from hyperscaler capex: optical EMS, InP/photodetector/laser supply, precision substrates, MLCCs and power components, switchgear and cooling subcomponents, testing/qualification vendors, and niche data/workflow automation platforms. This is an initial decomposition, not a security recommendation.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The market may still over-focus on GPUs and switches while underestimating the scarcity of qualified optical manufacturing partners that can assemble, test, and scale high-speed transceivers at acceptable yields.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer mid-cap EMS and optical manufacturing names with explicit 800G/1.6T datacenter commentary, rising optical revenue, backlog, or hyperscaler/NVIDIA ecosystem exposure. Avoid names where AI exposure is only implied by sector label.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: AI clusters require rapidly rising bandwidth between accelerators, racks, and data centers. As bandwidth shifts toward 800G and 1.6T optics, manufacturability, cleanroom capacity, yield, and customer qualification may become as important as chip supply.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: High-speed optical interconnects depend on specialized photonic materials and devices. If InP wafers, lasers, photodetectors, or precision substrates are capacity constrained, optical scaling can bottleneck AI networking even when GPU supply improves.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler AI training and inference capex requiring dense GPU/ASIC clusters, high-speed networking, storage, power, and cooling.
Shift from GPU-centric scaling toward mixed accelerator, custom ASIC, Ethernet, optical, and inference infrastructure.
AI model scaling increasing intra-cluster and inter-cluster bandwidth demand, pushing 800G and 1.6T optical transceiver adoption.
Rack-level power density growth increasing demand for power distribution, thermal management, passive components, and grid interconnection.
Enterprise and government adoption of AI software, automation, data platforms, and agentic workflow tooling.
Data-center electricity demand driving interest in nuclear, gas turbines, grid construction, transmission, transformers, backup power, and energy storage.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Use a two-lane Serenity funnel. Lane 1 maps reference leaders such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, Constellation, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta to define the demand signal. Lane 2 deliberately searches for underfollowed public suppliers with less obvious industry labels: optical contract manufacturers, photonics component makers, compound-semiconductor tools, passive-component specialists, power-conversion suppliers, grid-construction contractors, test/inspection vendors, data-center thermal component suppliers, niche AI workflow software, and regulated energy/fuel bottlenecks. Later layers should verify revenue exposure, customer concentration, backlog, capex, gross margin, analyst coverage, valuation, and customer dependency using filings and earnings calls.
supply_side_constraints: Advanced packaging, HBM integration, leading-edge foundry capacity, and high-end semiconductor equipment remain difficult to expand quickly.
Optical transceiver supply chains may be constrained by photonics components, InP wafers/devices, precision substrates, lasers, photodetectors, and qualified EMS capacity.
AI-server boards require dense high-reliability passive components, creating possible bottlenecks in high-capacitance, low-ESR, low-ESL MLCCs and power-delivery parts.
Data-center power infrastructure faces long lead times in switchgear, transformers, substations, grid interconnection, generators, turbines, and skilled construction labor.
Liquid cooling and high-density thermal systems require certification, reliability history, facility integration, and customer qualification.
AI software monetization is constrained by data readiness, security, workflow integration, procurement cycles, and proof of productivity ROI.
